g: stairs, riser, tread, staircase, stair code
a: US residential stairs: maximum riser 7¾ in, minimum tread 10 in, minimum headroom 6 ft 8 in, minimum width 36 in. A comfortable rule: 2 risers + 1 tread ≈ 24–25 in.

g: railing, guardrail, handrail, guard height
a: Guards are required where a walking surface is more than 30 in above the floor or grade below: at least 36 in high (42 in commercial), with openings that a 4 in sphere cannot pass. Handrails 34–38 in high.

g: door width, egress, exit, bedroom window
a: Each sleeping room needs an emergency escape opening: about 5.7 sq ft net clear, at least 20 in wide and 24 in high, sill no more than 44 in above the floor. The main exit door is at least 36 in wide.

g: ceiling height, room size, habitable
a: Habitable rooms need at least 7 ft ceiling height and 70 sq ft floor area (one dimension at least 7 ft) in the US IRC.

g: roof pitch, slope, rafter, gable, shingles
a: Pitch is rise per 12 in of run. Asphalt shingles need at least 2:12 (with extra underlayment below 4:12). Steeper roofs shed snow better. Use Roofs mode to generate rafters.

g: insulation, r value, u value, energy
s: IECC table R402.1.2 (varies by climate zone)
a: Required insulation depends on climate zone: typical US ceilings R-38 to R-60, walls R-13 to R-20+5. Air sealing matters as much as insulation thickness.

g: accessibility, ada, ramp, wheelchair
a: Ramps no steeper than 1:12 with landings every 30 in of rise, 36 in clear width, handrails on both sides above 6 in rise. Wheelchair turning needs a 60 in circle.

g: permit, building permit, inspection, zoning
a: Most structural, electrical, plumbing and many deck or fence jobs need a permit and inspections. Zoning controls setbacks, height and use. Always check your local building department.

g: patent, utility patent, patentable, invention
a: A utility patent protects how something works for about 20 years if it is new, useful and non-obvious. Public disclosure starts a 1-year grace period in the US but kills novelty in most other countries — file before showing it publicly.

g: provisional, ppa, patent pending
a: A US provisional application is cheaper, lets you say "patent pending" and holds your filing date for 12 months, but it must fully describe the invention and must be followed by a full application.

g: design patent, trademark, brand, logo
a: A design patent protects how something looks (15 years in the US). A trademark protects a brand name or logo used in commerce and can last indefinitely. Search existing marks before choosing a name.

g: copyright, cad files, software copyright
a: Copyright automatically protects original drawings, CAD files and code, but not the functional idea. Licence terms decide how others can use your files.

g: prior art, patent search, freedom to operate
a: Search Google Patents and Espacenet before investing. A freedom-to-operate check (by a patent attorney) tells you whether making the product infringes others' patents.

g: go to market, launch, sell, startup, crowdfunding
a: Validate demand first (talk to 20+ target customers, landing page or pre-orders), make a few units by hand, then crowdfund or sell small batches before tooling. Price for at least 3–5× unit cost.

g: nda, confidentiality, non disclosure
a: Use an NDA before showing an unpatented invention to manufacturers or partners. Many investors won't sign one, so share only what's needed.

g: print cost, filament cost, how much to print
s: cost = mass × filament price + machine time
a: Material cost ≈ grams × price per gram (PLA about $0.02–0.03/g). Add machine time (~$0.5–2 per hour hobby, $5+ service) and failed-print allowance. Ask "print cost 50 g" and I'll estimate.

g: cnc cost, machining cost, quote
a: CNC cost is mostly setup and machine time: number of setups, tight tolerances, deep pockets and hard materials raise price. Aluminium is cheapest to machine; stainless and titanium 2–4× more.

g: mold cost, tooling cost, injection cost
a: Aluminium prototype tools from about $2k–10k; steel production tools $10k–100k+. Piece price is then cents to dollars. Break-even against CNC/printing is often 500–2000 parts.

g: should cost, bom cost, retail price, markup
a: Retail price is often 3–5× bill-of-materials cost to cover assembly, packaging, distribution, retail margin and profit. Get real quotes early for anything over a few dollars.

g: volume, quantity break, economies of scale
a: Unit cost typically drops 10–20% every time quantity doubles (the learning curve), until tooling for a better process makes sense.

g: ohm, voltage, current, resistance, power, watts
a: Voltage equals current times resistance (V = I·R). Power is P = V·I = I²R = V²/R. Ask me "ohm's law 12 V 2 A" and I will calculate the rest.

g: led resistor, led, current limiting
a: R = (supply − LED forward voltage) / current. Typical forward voltage: red 2.0 V, green/blue/white 3.0 V; typical current 10–20 mA. Pick the next standard value up.

g: wire gauge, awg, ampacity, cable size, wire size
s: NEC table 310.16 (typical, 60–75 °C copper), chassis wiring tables
a: Typical copper ampacity in building wiring: 14 AWG 15 A, 12 AWG 20 A, 10 AWG 30 A, 8 AWG 40–50 A. Low-voltage chassis wiring can carry more but watch voltage drop; keep drop under about 3%.

g: voltage drop, long wire, cable run
a: Voltage drop = current × resistance per length × round-trip length. Copper is about 0.0172 Ω·mm²/m. For 12 V systems, voltage drop matters much more than for mains.

g: fuse, breaker, protection, short circuit
a: Size the fuse to protect the wire, not the device: the fuse rating must be at or below the wire's ampacity. Put it as close to the source as practical.

g: pcb, trace width, clearance, copper, ipc 2221
a: For 1 oz outer copper, a 0.25 mm trace carries about 0.75 A at 10 °C rise, 1 mm about 2.5 A. Keep decoupling capacitors (100 nF) right at each IC power pin and use a solid ground plane.

g: mains, 120v, 230v, isolation, creepage, earth
a: Mains voltage can kill. Keep about 6 mm creepage between mains and low voltage on a PCB, earth any exposed metal, use certified power supplies and fuses. Mains wiring in buildings must follow local electrical code and may require a licensed electrician.

g: battery, lithium, lipo, capacity, mah, runtime
a: Runtime is roughly capacity (mAh) divided by load current (mA), derated about 20%. Lithium cells need protection against over-charge, over-discharge and short circuit, and must not be punctured.

g: heat sink, thermal resistance, junction temperature
a: Junction temperature = ambient + power × thermal resistance. Keep silicon below about 125 °C (prefer < 85 °C). Use the app's Thermal button to estimate enclosure temperatures.

g: arduino, esp32, raspberry pi, microcontroller, gpio
a: Arduino Uno GPIO is 5 V, max about 20 mA per pin; ESP32 and Raspberry Pi are 3.3 V and not 5 V tolerant. Drive motors and relays through a transistor or driver with a flyback diode.

g: 3d print, fdm, overhang, wall thickness, print design
a: For FDM: walls at least 2–3 perimeters (≈1.2 mm), overhangs up to 45° without support, bridges under ~10 mm, holes print about 0.2 mm small, horizontal holes print better as teardrops. Orient so loads run along the layers, not across them.

g: sla, resin, sls, mjf, powder
a: SLA resin: walls ≥0.6 mm, add drain holes to hollow parts. SLS/MJF nylon: walls ≥0.8–1 mm, no supports needed, 0.3–0.5 mm clearance for moving parts printed in place.

g: cnc, milling, machining, inside corner, pocket
a: Inside vertical corners need a radius (at least the tool radius, ideally 1/3 of pocket depth). Keep pocket depth under about 4× tool diameter, walls ≥0.8 mm metal / 1.5 mm plastic, and use standard drill and thread sizes.

g: injection molding, moulding, draft, wall thickness, sink
a: Keep walls uniform (1–3 mm typical), add 1–2° draft, ribs 50–60% of wall thickness to avoid sink, radius all corners, and avoid undercuts unless you pay for side actions. Tooling costs thousands, so it pays off from about 1000+ parts.

g: casting, sand casting, die casting, investment
a: Sand casting suits low volume and large parts (draft 1–3°, rough finish). Die casting zinc/aluminium suits high volume with thin walls. Investment casting gives fine detail. Machine critical faces after casting.

g: sheet metal, bend radius, flange, k factor, bending
a: Inside bend radius at least equal to thickness; minimum flange length about 4× thickness; keep holes at least 2× thickness from bends; add bend reliefs. K-factor ≈ 0.33–0.45 for flat-pattern calculations.

g: welding, mig, tig, weld, fillet weld
a: MIG is fast and easy for steel; TIG is precise for thin and stainless/aluminium; stick works outdoors. Fillet weld throat = 0.707 × leg. Structural welds should be done and inspected to code by certified welders.

g: woodworking, joinery, mortise, dovetail, wood joint
a: Glue joints are strongest long-grain to long-grain. Mortise-and-tenon and dowels for frames, dovetails for drawers, pocket screws for quick cabinets. Pre-drill hardwood to avoid splitting.

g: surface finish, ra, roughness
a: Ra 3.2 µm is standard machined, 1.6 µm for fits and sealing, 0.8 µm or finer for bearings and sliding surfaces; tighter finishes cost more.

g: which process, how to make, manufacturing process, volume
a: 1–10 parts: 3D print or CNC. 10–1000: CNC, urethane casting, sheet metal. 1000+: injection moulding, die casting, stamping. Pick on volume, material and tolerance.

g: which material, material selection, choose material
s: Ashby, Materials Selection in Mechanical Design
a: Start from the main requirement: stiffness per weight (aluminium, carbon fibre), cheap strength (steel), corrosion resistance (stainless, plastics), heat (metals, PEEK) or easy printing (PLA, PETG). The app's material table lists yield strength, density and conductivity.

g: steel, mild steel, a36, s235, 1018, 4140
a: Mild steel (A36, S235) yields about 235–250 MPa; 1045 about 310–530 MPa; 4140 heat-treated 650+ MPa. Steel modulus is about 200 GPa regardless of grade, so stronger steel is not stiffer.

g: stainless, 304, 316, corrosion
a: 304 is the general-purpose grade; 316 adds molybdenum for salt water and chemicals. Stainless work-hardens and is harder to machine; yield about 205–215 MPa annealed.

g: aluminum, aluminium, 6061, 7075, 5052
a: 6061-T6 yields about 275 MPa and machines and welds well; 7075-T6 about 500 MPa but is hard to weld; 5052 bends well for sheet metal. Modulus is about 69 GPa, a third of steel.

g: pla, petg, abs, asa, nylon, tpu, filament
a: PLA is easy and stiff but softens near 55 °C. PETG is tougher and takes ~70 °C. ABS/ASA handle ~90 °C and outdoors (ASA). Nylon is tough and wear-resistant but absorbs water. TPU is flexible. Printed parts are weaker between layers (about 50–70% of in-plane strength).

g: wood, timber, plywood, oak, pine, grain
a: Wood is strong along the grain and weak across it. Spruce-pine-fir bending design value is around 875–1000 psi; oak is about twice as hard. Wood moves with humidity — allow for expansion across the grain.

g: corrosion, galvanic, rust, dissimilar metals
a: Dissimilar metals in contact with moisture corrode the less noble one: aluminium touching steel or copper corrodes. Isolate with washers, coatings or choose compatible metals.

g: thermal expansion, cte, expansion coefficient
s: ΔL = α·L·ΔT; typical α: steel 12, Al 23, PLA 68 µm/m·K
a: Length change = α × length × temperature change. Aluminium expands about twice as much as steel; plastics 5–10× steel.

g: fos, safety factor, margin, design factor
s: Shigley's Mechanical Engineering Design, ch.1; stddata.SAFETY_FACTORS
a: Factor of safety is allowable strength divided by working stress. Use about 1.5–2 for well-known loads and ductile metals, 2–3 for ordinary machine parts, 3–4 for uncertain loads or 3D-printed plastic, and higher for brittle materials, fatigue or anything that could hurt people.

g: torque, preload, tighten, bolt torque, nut factor
s: VDI 2230 simplified; T = K·F·d with K≈0.2 dry, 0.15 lubricated
a: Tightening torque is roughly T = K × F × d, where K is the nut factor (about 0.2 dry steel, 0.15 oiled), F the preload and d the nominal diameter. Aim for a preload of about 70–75% of proof load for reusable joints.

g: shear, bolt shear, single shear, double shear
a: A bolt in shear carries roughly 0.6 of its tensile strength over the stress area. Double shear doubles capacity. Better practice is to let clamping friction carry the load so the bolt does not slip into bearing.

g: thread engagement, tapped hole, how deep thread, engagement
a: Into steel, engage at least 1×d; into cast iron or brass about 1.5×d; into aluminium 2×d; into plastics use inserts or 2.5×d. More than about 1.5×d in steel adds little strength.

g: key, keyway, din 6885, parallel key
a: Parallel keys are sized from the shaft diameter (for example 20 mm shaft → 6×6 key). A keyway reduces shaft torsional strength; use a stress-concentration factor of about 0.75 on capacity. Key length is typically 1–1.5× shaft diameter.

g: bearing life, l10, dynamic load rating, bearing selection
a: Ball bearing life in millions of revolutions is L10 = (C/P)^3, where C is the dynamic rating and P the equivalent load; for rollers the exponent is 10/3. Hours = L10 × 10^6 / (60 × rpm).

g: gear, module, pitch diameter, gear ratio, involute
a: Pitch diameter = module × teeth. Centre distance = module × (z1 + z2) / 2. Ratio = z2/z1. Avoid fewer than about 17 teeth on a 20° spur gear or the root undercuts.

g: spring, spring rate, stiffness, compression spring
s: Shigley ch.10: k = G d^4 / (8 D^3 n)
a: Helical spring rate k = G·d⁴ / (8·D³·n) with G the shear modulus (79 GPa steel), d wire diameter, D mean coil diameter, n active coils. Keep spring index D/d between 4 and 12.

g: fatigue, endurance limit, cyclic, vibration
a: Steel has an endurance limit near half its tensile strength (before surface and size factors); aluminium and plastics have none and eventually fail at any cyclic stress. Sharp corners and holes concentrate stress 2–3×; use fillets.

g: fit, press fit, clearance fit, h7, g6, interference
a: Common hole-basis fits: H7/g6 sliding, H7/h6 locating clearance, H7/k6 transition, H7/p6 light press. For a 3D-printed hole, add about 0.2–0.3 mm to the nominal diameter for a slip fit.

g: stress concentration, kt, fillet radius, notch
a: Holes in a plate under tension raise local stress about 3×. Fillet radius of at least 10% of the smaller section size keeps Kt below about 1.7.

g: handle, grip diameter, ergonomics, hand
a: Power grip handles are most comfortable at 30–40 mm diameter and at least 100–120 mm long for a full hand (allow 125 mm with gloves). Finger clearance behind a pull handle at least 35 mm.

g: button size, touch target, finger
a: Make touch targets at least 9–10 mm (44 pt / 48 dp). Physical push buttons 10–19 mm diameter with 2–6 mm travel feel good; spacing at least 6 mm.

g: anthropometric, human dimensions, percentile, table height
a: Design for 5th-percentile female to 95th-percentile male. Seated desk height about 720–750 mm, seat height 400–520 mm adjustable, standing work surface about 950–1050 mm.

g: dfa, assembly, fewer parts, snap fit
s: Boothroyd & Dewhurst, Product Design for Manufacture and Assembly
a: Reduce part count, use self-locating features, make parts symmetric or obviously asymmetric, assemble from one direction (top-down), and prefer snap fits over loose screws where service allows.

g: snap fit, clip, cantilever snap
a: A cantilever snap's allowable strain is about 2% for PC/ABS and 4–5% for PP/nylon. Taper the beam and add a root radius to reduce stress.

g: prototype, iteration, mvp, design process
a: Sketch, then make crude looks-like and works-like prototypes fast, test with real users early, and iterate. Freeze the design only after the riskiest assumption is proven.

g: cmf, colour, finish, texture
a: Textured finishes (e.g. VDI 3400 / Mold-Tech) hide scratches and sink marks on moulded plastics. Matte surfaces show fingerprints less than gloss.

g: sustainable, recycle, eco, circular
a: Use a single recyclable material where possible, mark plastic resin codes, avoid glued mixed materials, design for repair (screws not glue) and keep parts small and light.

g: risk, hazard, fmea, risk assessment
a: List hazards, estimate severity × likelihood, then reduce risk in order: design it out, guard it, then warn. FMEA scores each failure mode by severity, occurrence and detection.

g: guard, pinch point, moving parts, machine safety
a: Guard pinch points, gears, belts and blades so fingers can't reach (a 6 mm gap needs about 10 mm reach distance; larger openings need much more). Add emergency stops on powered machines.

g: ce, ul, fcc, certification, compliance
s: EU New Legislative Framework; UL; FCC Part 15
a: Selling electronics typically needs CE (EU) or UL/ETL listing and FCC (US) for radio emissions. Toys, children's products and medical devices have extra strict rules.

g: children, toy safety, small parts, choking
a: Toys for under-3s must not have parts that fit in the small-parts cylinder (31.7 mm diameter). Avoid button batteries accessible to kids, sharp edges and lead.

g: lifting, working load limit, wll, rigging, hoist
a: Lifting gear uses a working load limit typically 1/5 of breaking strength (5:1) for rigging hardware, higher for wire rope. Never lift over people with homemade fixtures.

g: pressure vessel, compressed air, burst
a: Pressure vessels store dangerous energy; hoop stress = p·r/t. Use certified vessels for compressed air or gas — do not 3D print pressure vessels.

g: flammability, ul 94, fire, flame retardant
a: Enclosures around mains electronics should be UL 94 V-0 or V-1 rated plastic or metal. PLA and standard PETG are not flame-rated.

g: ppe, eye protection, goggles, workshop safety
a: Wear eye protection for any cutting, grinding or machining, hearing protection near loud tools, and a respirator for sanding, resin and welding fumes.

g: git, version control, commit, branch
a: Keep every project in git, commit small logical changes with clear messages, and work in branches. Never commit secrets such as API keys.

g: test, unit test, pytest, regression
a: Write automated tests for anything that must keep working; add a regression test every time you fix a bug. Fast unit tests plus a few end-to-end tests catch most problems.

g: api key, secret, password, credentials, env
a: Keep keys in environment variables or a secrets manager, never in source code or front-end JavaScript. Rotate a key immediately if it leaks.

g: security, sql injection, xss, validation, owasp
a: Treat all user input as untrusted: use parameterised SQL queries, escape output in HTML, check sizes and types, and run untrusted code only in a sandbox.

g: framework, language, stack, python, javascript
a: Pick the stack your team knows. Python suits data, CAD and back ends; JavaScript/TypeScript for web front ends; C/C++ or Rust for embedded and performance. Boring, well-documented tools beat new ones for products.

g: performance, slow, optimize, profiling
a: Measure before optimising: profile to find the real hot spot. Most speedups come from better algorithms, caching and avoiding repeated work, not micro-tweaks.

g: firmware, embedded, interrupt, watchdog
a: Keep interrupt handlers short, avoid dynamic memory in long-running firmware, enable a watchdog, and debounce mechanical buttons (about 10–50 ms).

g: license, mit, gpl, open source, licence
a: MIT and Apache-2.0 are permissive (keep the notice). GPL requires you to release your source if you distribute software containing GPL code. Check every dependency's licence before shipping a product.

g: deflection, beam, sag, simply supported, cantilever
s: Roark's Formulas for Stress and Strain, table 8.1
a: Simply supported, uniform load: δ = 5wL⁴/(384EI). Simply supported, centre point load: δ = PL³/(48EI). Cantilever, end load: δ = PL³/(3EI). Cantilever, uniform: δ = wL⁴/(8EI).

g: deflection limit, span over 360, l/360, serviceability
a: Floors usually limit live-load deflection to span/360, roofs span/240, and cantilevers or less sensitive items span/180. Brittle finishes such as tile may need span/480 or stiffer.

g: bending stress, section modulus, mc/i, flexure
s: σ = M/S, S = I/c (any mechanics text)
a: Bending stress σ = M / S where S is the section modulus. For a rectangle b×h, I = b·h³/12 and S = b·h²/6, so depth matters far more than width.

g: lumber, 2x4, 2x6, dimensional lumber, actual size
a: Nominal lumber is smaller than its name: a 2×4 is 1.5×3.5 in, 2×6 is 1.5×5.5 in, 2×8 is 1.5×7.25 in, 2×10 is 1.5×9.25 in, 2×12 is 1.5×11.25 in.

g: live load, dead load, floor load, snow load, psf
a: Residential floors are designed for about 40 psf live load (30 psf sleeping rooms), offices 50 psf, decks 40–60 psf. Dead load of a wood floor is roughly 10–15 psf. Snow load depends strongly on location; check local maps.

g: steel beam, ipe, w shape, i beam, wide flange
s: AISC Steel Construction Manual; EN 10365; stddata.IPE / WSHAPES
a: Wide-flange (W or IPE) sections are most efficient in bending about their strong axis. Pick by section modulus for strength and moment of inertia for deflection, then check lateral-torsional buckling if the compression flange is unbraced.

g: buckling, column, euler, slenderness
a: Euler buckling load P = π²EI / (K·L)², with K = 1 for pinned ends, 0.5 fixed–fixed, 2 for a flagpole. Slender columns fail by buckling well below the crushing stress.

g: concrete, rebar, cover, footing, psi
a: Normal concrete is 3000–4000 psi (20–30 MPa) and is strong in compression but weak in tension, so steel rebar takes tension. Typical cover is 1.5 in for interior, 3 in when cast against earth. Footings must reach below the local frost line.

g: wind load, seismic, lateral load, earthquake
a: Lateral loads from wind and earthquake govern tall or light structures. Wind pressure scales with the square of speed (q = 0.00256·V² psf, V in mph). Seismic design depends on site class and region; always use a licensed engineer.

g: truss, bridge, members, tension, compression
a: In a truss, members carry only axial tension or compression if loads act at joints. Top chords are usually in compression and need buckling checks; bottom chords in tension. Triangulation makes the frame rigid.

g: tolerance, general tolerance, iso 2768, default tolerance
a: ISO 2768-m (medium) gives ±0.1 mm up to 6 mm, ±0.2 mm 30–120 mm, ±0.3 mm 120–400 mm. Only tighten tolerances on features that actually need it — each step tighter costs more.

g: what tolerance can, achievable tolerance, precision
a: Typical achievable tolerance: FDM printing ±0.2–0.3 mm, SLA ±0.1 mm, CNC ±0.05 mm (±0.01 mm with care), sheet-metal bends ±0.25 mm, injection moulding ±0.1 mm, sand casting ±1 mm.

g: gd&t, gdt, geometric tolerance, feature control frame, datum
a: GD&T controls form, orientation, location and runout relative to datums. Datum A is usually the primary mounting face, B and C locate. Position tolerance on holes is better than ± coordinates because it gives a round tolerance zone 57% larger.

g: flatness, parallelism, perpendicularity, form tolerance
a: Flatness controls a surface by itself; parallelism and perpendicularity control orientation to a datum. Specify them on sealing faces, mounting faces and guides.

g: mmc, lmc, bonus tolerance
a: MMC (Ⓜ) lets position tolerance grow as a hole gets bigger from its smallest size — bonus tolerance — which cheaply guarantees bolts still fit.

g: stack up, tolerance stack, worst case, rss
a: Worst-case stack adds all tolerances; RSS (root sum of squares) is a realistic statistical estimate for many parts. Reduce the number of parts in the chain to cut the stack.
